- Human Habitat-Change Agents: Human beings represented collectively through logging, burning, agriculture, road construction, settlements, illegal hunting, and habitat conversion in the Amazon. The screenplay provides no stable physical appearance, clothing, age, sex, or individual identity, so this entity is defined only as a recurring human group associated with landscape transformation.
- Black Caiman: Melanosuchus niger, a very large Amazonian crocodilian adapted to slow-moving rivers, lakes, swamps, and flooded forests. A large male may exceed 5 meters in length. It has dark skin, heavy bony osteoderms forming protective armor along the back and sides, conical gripping teeth, a powerful tail, and eyes and nostrils positioned on top of the head for remaining mostly submerged. Adult and juvenile individuals are both referenced: juveniles are substantially smaller and have thinner armor, while large adults are among the dominant freshwater predators. No individual-specific scars or markings are established.
</subjects>

<action>
A protected river landscape extends beyond a boundary marker as the black caiman surfaces in the restored habitat.
</action>

<environment>
Amazonian wetland with slow water, flooded forest, and intact shoreline vegetation.
</environment>

<camera>
Wide environmental shot from the riverbank, linking habitat protection with the animal’s return.
</camera>

<style>
Ultra-realistic premium wildlife documentary imagery with authentic animal anatomy, natural behavior, realistic scale, physically believable environments, and convincing animal biomechanics.

The visual language should resemble footage captured for a world-class natural-history documentary using professional full-frame cinema cameras, high-end wildlife cameras, long telephoto lenses, and experienced field cinematography.

REALISM IS THE PRIMARY RULE.

Cinematic intensity must come from real animal behavior, timing, physical interaction, environmental reaction, camera placement, and composition — never from fantasy exaggeration.

==================================================
EXPOSURE AND IMAGE QUALITY
==========================

Use bright, clean, natural exposure with clearly readable animals and environmental detail.

Avoid excessively dark, muddy, underexposed, or crushed-shadow imagery.

Preserve realistic highlights and shadows while maintaining strong local contrast and clear separation between subjects and background.

Daytime scenes should feel naturally luminous, with believable sunlight filtered through clouds, foliage, mist, dust, rain, humidity, or atmospheric haze when appropriate.

Maintain high photographic detail in fur, feathers, scales, skin, eyes, vegetation, soil, rock, snow, mud, and water.

==================================================
COLOR
=====

Colors must remain natural, rich, and believable.

Use:

* accurate fur and feather coloration;
* realistic vegetation greens;
* natural earth tones;
* physically believable water and sky colors;
* subtle cinematic color treatment.

Avoid:

* extreme teal-and-orange grading;
* oversaturation;
* neon colors;
* fantasy coloration;
* artificial glow;
* heavy bloom;
* exaggerated HDR appearance.

==================================================
ANIMAL ANATOMY
==============

Subjects must remain anatomically accurate and species-appropriate.

Preserve:

* correct body proportions;
* correct limb count;
* species-specific skeletal structure;
* realistic head and facial anatomy;
* correct paws, hooves, claws, horns, tusks, wings, fins, tails, and jaws;
* accurate fur, feathers, scales, skin, and markings;
* believable size and age characteristics;
* natural posture.

Animals must not display human-like facial expressions, gestures, emotional acting, or theatrical poses.

==================================================
ANIMAL BEHAVIOR
===============

All behavior must remain consistent with real wildlife behavior.

Do not create aggression merely for spectacle.

However, when a shot explicitly depicts predation, territorial conflict, competition, defense, pursuit, escape, or fighting, DO NOT automatically soften the behavior.

Realistic wildlife conflict may be sudden, explosive, forceful, chaotic, and dangerous.

Intensity is allowed and encouraged when biologically and narratively justified.

The animals should behave like real animals under pressure, not like actors performing a staged fight.

Species-specific behavior must determine:

* stance;
* attack distance;
* acceleration;
* reaction timing;
* defensive movement;
* striking method;
* biting behavior;
* grappling behavior;
* use of horns, claws, jaws, paws, wings, tails, or body mass;
* retreat behavior;
* pursuit behavior;
* dominance behavior.

Avoid repetitive generic lunging or endless artificial aggression.

==================================================
HIGH-INTENSITY PHYSICAL INTERACTION
===================================

During chases, attacks, escapes, territorial contests, or physical struggles, preserve believable speed, weight, momentum, balance, inertia, and reaction time.

High-energy movement should visibly show appropriate biomechanics:

* muscles loading before acceleration;
* hindquarters driving movement;
* paws, claws, hooves, or feet gripping the terrain;
* bodies leaning into turns;
* realistic braking;
* shifting center of gravity;
* rapid defensive pivots;
* missed strikes carrying momentum past the target;
* bodies recoiling after contact;
* temporary loss of balance;
* immediate attempts to recover footing.

Physical contact must feel heavy and real.

When animals collide, strike, shove, bite, block, grapple, or brush against one another, show realistic transfer of force.

Appropriate details may include:

* fur or feathers compressing at contact;
* skin and muscle reacting to impact;
* bodies shifting from transferred momentum;
* feet sliding or digging into the ground;
* shoulders, hips, necks, or torsos rotating naturally;
* immediate recoil;
* stumbling;
* twisting;
* scrambling to regain balance.

Do not make bodies behave like weightless objects, rigid models, rubber, or game characters.

==================================================
NEAR-MISSES AND REACTIONS
=========================

Not every dramatic wildlife moment requires successful contact.

Realistic tension may come from:

* a bite narrowly missing;
* horns passing beside an opponent;
* a paw strike missing by centimeters;
* prey changing direction at the last instant;
* a predator overshooting;
* an animal stumbling while escaping;
* a defensive turn interrupting an attack;
* a brief hesitation before recommitting.

These moments should retain realistic reaction speed and species-appropriate movement.

==================================================
ENVIRONMENTAL INTERACTION
=========================

The environment must respond naturally to animal movement.

Depending on habitat and action, this may include:

* dust kicked from dry soil;
* dirt displaced by paws or hooves;
* loose gravel scattering;
* mud splashing;
* water displacement and spray;
* snow spraying;
* grass flattening beneath bodies;
* vegetation shaking after contact;
* branches moving;
* leaves falling;
* ripples, wakes, or waves forming;
* footprints, disturbed ground, or temporary debris movement.

Environmental response must always be proportional to animal size, speed, and physical force.

Avoid exaggerated Hollywood explosions of dust, water, mud, vegetation, or debris.

==================================================
ENVIRONMENT
===========

Habitats must feel ecologically plausible, physically real, richly detailed, and naturally integrated with the subjects.

Vegetation, terrain, water, weather, atmospheric conditions, and background wildlife must match the intended habitat.

Maintain realistic depth, perspective, scale, and spatial relationships.

Do not create decorative environmental elements merely to make the frame more cinematic.

==================================================
CINEMATOGRAPHY
==============

Use cinematic but believable wildlife cinematography.

Favor:

* strong subject readability;
* clear foreground-midground-background separation;
* realistic lens compression;
* purposeful composition;
* professional telephoto framing;
* believable camera placement;
* natural depth;
* readable spatial relationships between animals.

Calm behavior may use:

* static observation;
* slow tracking;
* gentle push-ins;
* restrained pans or tilts.

Fast and unpredictable behavior may use more reactive cinematography:

* controlled handheld tracking;
* urgent but professional panning;
* rapid reframing to maintain the subject;
* telephoto tracking with slight natural operator correction;
* animals temporarily approaching frame edges during sudden movement;
* short periods of realistic field-camera instability during explosive action.

The camera should feel like an experienced wildlife cinematographer trying to follow an unpredictable real event.

Do not make every action shot perfectly centered or mechanically stabilized.

A small amount of motivated camera imperfection can improve documentary authenticity.

Avoid:

* artificial spinning;
* dramatic orbiting;
* impossible camera movement;
* extreme crash zooms;
* excessive shake;
* artificial speed ramps;
* random reframing;
* fisheye distortion;
* unrealistic depth of field;
* excessive lens flare.

==================================================
MOTION
======

For video, animal motion must remain temporally coherent and physically plausible.

Movement should show continuous momentum from frame to frame.

During rapid action, preserve:

* body orientation;
* limb sequence;
* direction of travel;
* subject identity;
* relative distance;
* realistic acceleration and deceleration.

Animals must not:

* teleport;
* slide unnaturally;
* float;
* instantly reverse momentum;
* snap between poses;
* change body size;
* change anatomy;
* duplicate;
* disappear;
* morph into another animal.

==================================================
TEMPORAL CONSISTENCY
====================

Maintain high temporal consistency.

Subjects must retain:

* species;
* markings;
* body proportions;
* size;
* age characteristics;
* fur or feather patterns;
* injuries or persistent identifying features when established.

Background terrain, vegetation, lighting, shadows, weather, and environmental objects must not flicker, warp, teleport, or transform unexpectedly.

==================================================
SCENE CONTINUITY
================

Lighting direction, weather, time of day, environmental characteristics, subject appearance, relative scale, terrain, and overall color treatment must remain visually consistent across shots belonging to the same continuous scene.

Animal positions and movement direction should also preserve logical spatial continuity between consecutive shots.

==================================================
ALWAYS PRESERVE
===============

* Ultra-realistic wildlife documentary realism
* Accurate animal anatomy
* Species-appropriate behavior
* Realistic body weight and biomechanics
* Convincing momentum and physical contact
* Realistic reactions and recovery after impact
* Believable environmental interaction
* Authentic habitats
* Natural color
* Bright, clean exposure
* Professional wildlife cinematography
* High photographic detail
* Clear subject readability
* Stable identity and markings
* Consistent scale
* Logical spatial continuity

==================================================
AVOID
=====

* Cartoon, illustration, anime, CGI-looking, or game-like imagery
* Fantasy behavior
* Human-like animal acting
* Anatomical deformation
* Extra limbs
* Morphing
* Duplication
* Disappearing subjects
* Identity changes
* Weightless bodies
* Rubber-like movement
* Sliding feet
* Impossible acceleration
* Impossible jumps
* Repetitive theatrical attacks
* Unmotivated aggression
* Unrealistic animal behavior
* Oversaturated colors
* Neon coloration
* Excessive darkness
* Crushed shadows
* Artificial glow
* Heavy bloom
* Extreme cinematic grading
* Unrealistic depth of field
* Unmotivated camera movement
* Excessive shake
* Lighting flicker
* Background warping
* Environmental instability
* Text
* Subtitles
* Logos
* Borders
* Watermarks

</style>

Use bright, clean, natural exposure with clearly readable animals and environmental detail.

Avoid excessively dark, muddy, underexposed, or crushed-shadow imagery.

Preserve realistic highlights and shadows while maintaining strong local contrast and clear separation between subjects and background.

Daytime scenes should feel naturally luminous, with believable sunlight filtered through clouds, foliage, mist, dust, rain, humidity, or atmospheric haze when appropriate.

Maintain high photographic detail in fur, feathers, scales, skin, eyes, vegetation, soil, rock, snow, mud, and water.

==================================================
COLOR
=====

Colors must remain natural, rich, and believable.

Use:

* accurate fur and feather coloration;
* realistic vegetation greens;
* natural earth tones;
* physically believable water and sky colors;
* subtle cinematic color treatment.

Avoid:

* extreme teal-and-orange grading;
* oversaturation;
* neon colors;
* fantasy coloration;
* artificial glow;
* heavy bloom;
* exaggerated HDR appearance.

==================================================
ANIMAL ANATOMY
==============

Subjects must remain anatomically accurate and species-appropriate.

Preserve:

* correct body proportions;
* correct limb count;
* species-specific skeletal structure;
* realistic head and facial anatomy;
* correct paws, hooves, claws, horns, tusks, wings, fins, tails, and jaws;
* accurate fur, feathers, scales, skin, and markings;
* believable size and age characteristics;
* natural posture.

Animals must not display human-like facial expressions, gestures, emotional acting, or theatrical poses.

==================================================
ANIMAL BEHAVIOR
===============

All behavior must remain consistent with real wildlife behavior.

Do not create aggression merely for spectacle.

However, when a shot explicitly depicts predation, territorial conflict, competition, defense, pursuit, escape, or fighting, DO NOT automatically soften the behavior.

Realistic wildlife conflict may be sudden, explosive, forceful, chaotic, and dangerous.

Intensity is allowed and encouraged when biologically and narratively justified.

The animals should behave like real animals under pressure, not like actors performing a staged fight.

Species-specific behavior must determine:

* stance;
* attack distance;
* acceleration;
* reaction timing;
* defensive movement;
* striking method;
* biting behavior;
* grappling behavior;
* use of horns, claws, jaws, paws, wings, tails, or body mass;
* retreat behavior;
* pursuit behavior;
* dominance behavior.

Avoid repetitive generic lunging or endless artificial aggression.

==================================================
HIGH-INTENSITY PHYSICAL INTERACTION
===================================

During chases, attacks, escapes, territorial contests, or physical struggles, preserve believable speed, weight, momentum, balance, inertia, and reaction time.

High-energy movement should visibly show appropriate biomechanics:

* muscles loading before acceleration;
* hindquarters driving movement;
* paws, claws, hooves, or feet gripping the terrain;
* bodies leaning into turns;
* realistic braking;
* shifting center of gravity;
* rapid defensive pivots;
* missed strikes carrying momentum past the target;
* bodies recoiling after contact;
* temporary loss of balance;
* immediate attempts to recover footing.

Physical contact must feel heavy and real.

When animals collide, strike, shove, bite, block, grapple, or brush against one another, show realistic transfer of force.

Appropriate details may include:

* fur or feathers compressing at contact;
* skin and muscle reacting to impact;
* bodies shifting from transferred momentum;
* feet sliding or digging into the ground;
* shoulders, hips, necks, or torsos rotating naturally;
* immediate recoil;
* stumbling;
* twisting;
* scrambling to regain balance.

Do not make bodies behave like weightless objects, rigid models, rubber, or game characters.

=========================

Not every dramatic wildlife moment requires successful contact.

Realistic tension may come from:

* a bite narrowly missing;
* horns passing beside an opponent;
* a paw strike missing by centimeters;
* prey changing direction at the last instant;
* a predator overshooting;
* an animal stumbling while escaping;
* a defensive turn interrupting an attack;
* a brief hesitation before recommitting.

These moments should retain realistic reaction speed and species-appropriate movement.

=========================

* dust kicked from dry soil;
* dirt displaced by paws or hooves;
* loose gravel scattering;
* mud splashing;
* water displacement and spray;
* snow spraying;
* grass flattening beneath bodies;
* vegetation shaking after contact;
* branches moving;
* leaves falling;
* ripples, wakes, or waves forming;
* footprints, disturbed ground, or temporary debris movement.

Avoid exaggerated Hollywood explosions of dust, water, mud, vegetation, or debris.

===========

Vegetation, terrain, water, weather, atmospheric conditions, and background wildlife must match the intended habitat.

Maintain realistic depth, perspective, scale, and spatial relationships.

Do not create decorative environmental elements merely to make the frame more cinematic.

==================================================

==============

Use cinematic but believable wildlife cinematography.

Favor:

* strong subject readability;
* clear foreground-midground-background separation;
* realistic lens compression;
* purposeful composition;
* professional telephoto framing;
* believable camera placement;
* natural depth;
* readable spatial relationships between animals.

* static observation;
* slow tracking;
* gentle push-ins;
* restrained pans or tilts.

* controlled handheld tracking;
* urgent but professional panning;
* rapid reframing to maintain the subject;
* telephoto tracking with slight natural operator correction;

* short periods of realistic field-camera instability during explosive action.

* dramatic orbiting;
* impossible camera movement;
* extreme crash zooms;
* excessive shake;
* artificial speed ramps;
* random reframing;
* fisheye distortion;
* unrealistic depth of field;
* excessive lens flare.

==================================================

======

For video, animal motion must remain temporally coherent and physically plausible.

Movement should show continuous momentum from frame to frame.

During rapid action, preserve:

* body orientation;
* limb sequence;
* direction of travel;
* subject identity;
* relative distance;
* realistic acceleration and deceleration.

Animals must not:

* teleport;
* slide unnaturally;
* float;
* instantly reverse momentum;
* snap between poses;
* change body size;
* change anatomy;
* duplicate;
* disappear;
* morph into another animal.

* age characteristics;
* fur or feather patterns;

* striking method;

* pursuit behavior;

* hindquarters driving movement;
* paws, claws, hooves, or feet gripping the terrain;
* bodies leaning into turns;
* realistic braking;
* shifting center of gravity;
* rapid defensive pivots;
* missed strikes carrying momentum past the target;
* bodies recoiling after contact;

* physically believable water and sky colors;

* extreme teal-and-orange grading;
* oversaturation;
* neon colors;
* fantasy coloration;
* artificial glow;
* heavy bloom;
* exaggerated HDR appearance.

==============

Preserve:

* correct body proportions;
* correct limb count;
* species-specific skeletal structure;
* realistic head and facial anatomy;
* correct paws, hooves, claws, horns, tusks, wings, fins, tails, and jaws;
* accurate fur, feathers, scales, skin, and markings;
* believable size and age characteristics;
* natural posture.

===============

All behavior must remain consistent with real wildlife behavior.

Do not create aggression merely for spectacle.

However, when a shot explicitly depicts predation, territorial conflict, competition, defense, pursuit, escape, or fighting, DO NOT automatically soften the behavior.

Realistic wildlife conflict may be sudden, explosive, forceful, chaotic, and dangerous.

Intensity is allowed and encouraged when biologically and narratively justified.

The animals should behave like real animals under pressure, not like actors performing a staged fight.

Species-specific behavior must determine:

* stance;
* attack distance;
* acceleration;
* reaction timing;
* defensive movement;
* striking method;
* biting behavior;
* grappling behavior;
* use of horns, claws, jaws, paws, wings, tails, or body mass;
* retreat behavior;
* pursuit behavior;
* dominance behavior.

===================================

* muscles loading before acceleration;
* hindquarters driving movement;
* paws, claws, hooves, or feet gripping the terrain;
* bodies leaning into turns;
* realistic braking;
* shifting center of gravity;
* rapid defensive pivots;
* missed strikes carrying momentum past the target;
* bodies recoiling after contact;
* temporary loss of balance;
* immediate attempts to recover footing.

* feet sliding or digging into the ground;

* immediate recoil;
* stumbling;
* twisting;
* scrambling to regain balance.

<style>
Ultra-realistic premium wildlife documentary imagery with authentic animal anatomy, natural behavior, realistic scale, physically believable environments, and convincing animal biomechanics.

The visual language should resemble footage captured for a world-class natural-history documentary using professional full-frame cinema cameras, high-end wildlife cameras, long telephoto lenses, and experienced field cinematography.

REALISM IS THE PRIMARY RULE.

Cinematic intensity must come from real animal behavior, timing, physical interaction, environmental reaction, camera placement, and composition — never from fantasy exaggeration.

==================================================
EXPOSURE AND IMAGE QUALITY
==========================

Use bright, clean, natural exposure with clearly readable animals and environmental detail.

Avoid excessively dark, muddy, underexposed, or crushed-shadow imagery.

Preserve realistic highlights and shadows while maintaining strong local contrast and clear separation between subjects and background.

Daytime scenes should feel naturally luminous, with believable sunlight filtered through clouds, foliage, mist, dust, rain, humidity, or atmospheric haze when appropriate.

Maintain high photographic detail in fur, feathers, scales, skin, eyes, vegetation, soil, rock, snow, mud, and water.

==================================================
COLOR
=====

Colors must remain natural, rich, and believable.

Use:

* accurate fur and feather coloration;
* realistic vegetation greens;
* natural earth tones;
* physically believable water and sky colors;
* subtle cinematic color treatment.

Avoid:

* extreme teal-and-orange grading;
* oversaturation;
* neon colors;
* fantasy coloration;
* artificial glow;
* heavy bloom;
* exaggerated HDR appearance.

==================================================
ANIMAL ANATOMY
==============

Subjects must remain anatomically accurate and species-appropriate.

Preserve:

* correct body proportions;
* correct limb count;
* species-specific skeletal structure;
* realistic head and facial anatomy;
* correct paws, hooves, claws, horns, tusks, wings, fins, tails, and jaws;
* accurate fur, feathers, scales, skin, and markings;
* believable size and age characteristics;
* natural posture.

Animals must not display human-like facial expressions, gestures, emotional acting, or theatrical poses.

==================================================
ANIMAL BEHAVIOR
===============

All behavior must remain consistent with real wildlife behavior.

Do not create aggression merely for spectacle.

However, when a shot explicitly depicts predation, territorial conflict, competition, defense, pursuit, escape, or fighting, DO NOT automatically soften the behavior.

Realistic wildlife conflict may be sudden, explosive, forceful, chaotic, and dangerous.

Intensity is allowed and encouraged when biologically and narratively justified.

The animals should behave like real animals under pressure, not like actors performing a staged fight.

Species-specific behavior must determine:

* stance;
* attack distance;
* acceleration;
* reaction timing;
* defensive movement;
* striking method;
* biting behavior;
* grappling behavior;
* use of horns, claws, jaws, paws, wings, tails, or body mass;
* retreat behavior;
* pursuit behavior;
* dominance behavior.

Avoid repetitive generic lunging or endless artificial aggression.

==================================================
HIGH-INTENSITY PHYSICAL INTERACTION
===================================

During chases, attacks, escapes, territorial contests, or physical struggles, preserve believable speed, weight, momentum, balance, inertia, and reaction time.

High-energy movement should visibly show appropriate biomechanics:

* muscles loading before acceleration;
* hindquarters driving movement;
* paws, claws, hooves, or feet gripping the terrain;
* bodies leaning into turns;
* realistic braking;
* shifting center of gravity;
* rapid defensive pivots;
* missed strikes carrying momentum past the target;
* bodies recoiling after contact;
* temporary loss of balance;
* immediate attempts to recover footing.

Physical contact must feel heavy and real.

When animals collide, strike, shove, bite, block, grapple, or brush against one another, show realistic transfer of force.

Appropriate details may include:

* fur or feathers compressing at contact;
* skin and muscle reacting to impact;
* bodies shifting from transferred momentum;
* feet sliding or digging into the ground;
* shoulders, hips, necks, or torsos rotating naturally;
* immediate recoil;
* stumbling;
* twisting;
* scrambling to regain balance.

Do not make bodies behave like weightless objects, rigid models, rubber, or game characters.

==================================================
NEAR-MISSES AND REACTIONS
=========================

Not every dramatic wildlife moment requires successful contact.

Realistic tension may come from:

* a bite narrowly missing;
* horns passing beside an opponent;
* a paw strike missing by centimeters;
* prey changing direction at the last instant;
* a predator overshooting;
* an animal stumbling while escaping;
* a defensive turn interrupting an attack;
* a brief hesitation before recommitting.

These moments should retain realistic reaction speed and species-appropriate movement.

==================================================
ENVIRONMENTAL INTERACTION
=========================

The environment must respond naturally to animal movement.

Depending on habitat and action, this may include:

* dust kicked from dry soil;
* dirt displaced by paws or hooves;
* loose gravel scattering;
* mud splashing;
* water displacement and spray;
* snow spraying;
* grass flattening beneath bodies;
* vegetation shaking after contact;
* branches moving;
* leaves falling;
* ripples, wakes, or waves forming;
* footprints, disturbed ground, or temporary debris movement.

Environmental response must always be proportional to animal size, speed, and physical force.

Avoid exaggerated Hollywood explosions of dust, water, mud, vegetation, or debris.

==================================================
ENVIRONMENT
===========

Habitats must feel ecologically plausible, physically real, richly detailed, and naturally integrated with the subjects.

Vegetation, terrain, water, weather, atmospheric conditions, and background wildlife must match the intended habitat.

Maintain realistic depth, perspective, scale, and spatial relationships.

Do not create decorative environmental elements merely to make the frame more cinematic.

==================================================
CINEMATOGRAPHY
==============

Use cinematic but believable wildlife cinematography.

Favor:

* strong subject readability;
* clear foreground-midground-background separation;
* realistic lens compression;
* purposeful composition;
* professional telephoto framing;
* believable camera placement;
* natural depth;
* readable spatial relationships between animals.

Calm behavior may use:

* static observation;
* slow tracking;
* gentle push-ins;
* restrained pans or tilts.

Fast and unpredictable behavior may use more reactive cinematography:

* controlled handheld tracking;
* urgent but professional panning;
* rapid reframing to maintain the subject;
* telephoto tracking with slight natural operator correction;
* animals temporarily approaching frame edges during sudden movement;
* short periods of realistic field-camera instability during explosive action.

The camera should feel like an experienced wildlife cinematographer trying to follow an unpredictable real event.

Do not make every action shot perfectly centered or mechanically stabilized.

A small amount of motivated camera imperfection can improve documentary authenticity.

Avoid:

* artificial spinning;
* dramatic orbiting;
* impossible camera movement;
* extreme crash zooms;
* excessive shake;
* artificial speed ramps;
* random reframing;
* fisheye distortion;
* unrealistic depth of field;
* excessive lens flare.

==================================================
MOTION
======

For video, animal motion must remain temporally coherent and physically plausible.

Movement should show continuous momentum from frame to frame.

During rapid action, preserve:

* body orientation;
* limb sequence;
* direction of travel;
* subject identity;
* relative distance;
* realistic acceleration and deceleration.

Animals must not:

* teleport;
* slide unnaturally;
* float;
* instantly reverse momentum;
* snap between poses;
* change body size;
* change anatomy;
* duplicate;
* disappear;
* morph into another animal.

==================================================
TEMPORAL CONSISTENCY
====================

Maintain high temporal consistency.

Subjects must retain:

* species;
* markings;
* body proportions;
* size;
* age characteristics;
* fur or feather patterns;
* injuries or persistent identifying features when established.

Background terrain, vegetation, lighting, shadows, weather, and environmental objects must not flicker, warp, teleport, or transform unexpectedly.

==================================================
SCENE CONTINUITY
================

Lighting direction, weather, time of day, environmental characteristics, subject appearance, relative scale, terrain, and overall color treatment must remain visually consistent across shots belonging to the same continuous scene.

Animal positions and movement direction should also preserve logical spatial continuity between consecutive shots.
